title: Mali and Mansa Musa
text: In the fourteenth century, the Mali Empire controlled important routes carrying gold and salt across West Africa. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca displayed enormous wealth and connected Mali to a wider scholarly world. Timbuktu became known for trade and learning, though its history reaches beyond any single ruler.
context: An introduction to medieval Mali and trans-Saharan exchange.
vocabulary: pilgrimage: a journey to a sacred place
scholarly: related to serious study

title: Ideas in Song China
text: During China's Song dynasty, printers produced books with carved blocks and movable type. Engineers improved clocks, ships, canals, and iron production. Merchants used paper money on a large scale. These developments did not appear all at once, but together they reveal a complex and inventive society.
context: A broad overview of selected Song-era innovations.
vocabulary: dynasty: a succession of rulers from one family
movable type: reusable characters for printing

title: Roads Across the Andes
text: The Inca governed a vast Andean realm without wheeled transport or a conventional written script. Roads, bridges, runners, storehouses, and knotted records called quipu helped connect high mountains and valleys. Their achievement depended on organized labor, while imperial rule also placed heavy demands on conquered communities.
context: An introduction to Inca administration before Spanish conquest.
vocabulary: Andean: relating to the Andes Mountains
quipu: knotted cords used for records

title: Reading an Ocean
text: Polynesian navigators crossed immense stretches of the Pacific using stars, winds, currents, clouds, birds, and patterns of ocean swell. Their knowledge was learned through careful teaching and experience. Navigation joined observation with memory, proving that a map can exist in trained understanding as well as on paper.
context: A respectful overview of traditional Pacific wayfinding.
vocabulary: swell: long rolling waves
wayfinding: determining and following a route

title: The Translation Movement
text: Scholars working in Abbasid Baghdad translated and studied writings from Greek, Persian, Indian, and other traditions. They did more than preserve old books: they criticized, extended, and reorganized knowledge in mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and philosophy. Later scholars in many regions built on this work.
context: An overview of scholarship centered in Baghdad from the eighth to tenth centuries.
vocabulary: Abbasid: relating to a major Islamic caliphate
astronomy: scientific study of space

title: Haiti Wins Independence
text: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue began a revolution in 1791. After years of conflict, Haiti declared independence in 1804 and abolished slavery. The revolution challenged empires that proclaimed liberty while profiting from bondage. Its leaders and factions had complex aims and fierce disagreements.
context: A non-graphic summary of the Haitian Revolution.
vocabulary: colony: territory controlled by another country
abolished: formally ended

title: Streets and Drains of Mohenjo-daro
text: Mohenjo-daro was a major city of the Indus civilization more than four thousand years ago. Builders laid out streets in blocks and connected many homes to brick drains and wells. Standard-sized bricks suggest shared planning, although no surviving text explains who directed it. The Indus script has not been confidently deciphered, so archaeology carries much of the evidence. The city's design reveals skilled cooperation without proving that its government matched any familiar modern system.
context: An evidence-based account that distinguishes impressive planning from guesses about Indus government.
vocabulary: deciphered: worked out so that writing can be read
archaeology: study of the past through material remains
source: Original summary based on UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro

references.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro

title: Aksum Connects Three Regions
text: The kingdom of Aksum grew in the highlands of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea. Its Red Sea port of Adulis linked African trade routes with Arabia, the Mediterranean, and the Indian Ocean. Aksumite rulers issued coins in gold, silver, and bronze, sometimes using Greek inscriptions for wide audiences. In the fourth century CE, royal coins began displaying the Christian cross. Coins cannot describe every person's life, but their metal, language, and symbols provide compact evidence of trade and political change.
context: Aksum presented through African geography, trade networks, coinage, and religious change.
vocabulary: inscription: words written or carved on an object
coinage: a system of coins issued by a government
source: Original summary based on The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Monumental Architecture and Stelae of the Aksumite Empire

references.citation: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Monumental Architecture and Stelae of the Aksumite Empire

title: Water and Power at Angkor
text: From the ninth to the fifteenth century, Angkor was the center of the Khmer Empire in what is now Cambodia. Temples such as Angkor Wat stood within a much larger inhabited landscape. Reservoirs, canals, embankments, and rice fields managed water across changing wet and dry seasons. Scholars still debate exactly how every part of this network functioned and how water problems contributed to political change. New surveys have revealed roads and settlement patterns hidden by vegetation. Angkor's history is therefore not a tale of a mysterious lost city, but of generations who engineered, maintained, altered, and eventually left a complex urban region.
context: A modern archaeological view of Angkor as an inhabited landscape, not only a group of temples.
vocabulary: reservoir: a place where water is stored
embankment: a raised bank built to hold back water or support a road
source: Original summary based on UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Angkor

title: Messages Across the Mongol Empire
text: Mongol rulers supported a relay network often called the yam. Stations along major routes kept fresh horses, supplies, and shelter for authorized messengers. A tablet or document identified a traveler's right to use the system. By changing mounts, envoys could carry orders and reports far faster than one tired horse could travel. Merchants and diplomats also benefited from guarded routes, though safety varied by time and place. The network did not erase the violence of Mongol conquest; it shows how administration helped hold vast territories together after armies had crossed them.
context: The Mongol relay system presented as infrastructure for government and exchange.
vocabulary: relay: a system in which one carrier or horse replaces another
envoy: an official messenger or representative
source: Original summary based on The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Legacy of Genghis Khan

references.citation: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Legacy of Genghis Khan

title: Stone Walls of Great Zimbabwe
text: Between about 1100 and 1450 CE, Great Zimbabwe became a major political and trading center in southern Africa. Skilled builders fitted granite blocks into high, curving walls without mortar. Cattle wealth and farming supported the community, while glass beads, imported ceramics, and gold routes connected it with Indian Ocean commerce. European colonizers once denied that Africans had built the site, despite clear evidence, because racism shaped their conclusions. Archaeology has firmly restored Great Zimbabwe to the history of Shona-speaking peoples. The ruins show how evidence can correct both missing records and deliberately biased stories.
context: An account of Great Zimbabwe that addresses trade, engineering, and the racist denial of African authorship.
vocabulary: mortar: material used to bind stones or bricks
biased: unfairly shaped toward one conclusion
source: Original summary based on The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Great Zimbabwe (11th–15th Century)

references.citation: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Great Zimbabwe (11th–15th Century)

title: Akbar's Court of Many Arguments
text: The Mughal emperor Akbar ruled much of South Asia from 1556 to 1605. He built alliances with Rajput rulers, ended a tax placed on non-Muslim subjects, and invited Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian, and Christian thinkers to debate at court. Translation projects made Sanskrit works available in Persian, the language of administration. These policies supported a diverse empire, but they did not create modern equality: Akbar remained an absolute monarch who expanded through war and demanded revenue. Court histories also praised their patron, so they require careful reading. His reign shows how curiosity and inclusion can serve genuine learning, political stability, and imperial power at the same time.
context: A balanced interpretation of Akbar's religious discussions, translations, alliances, and imperial authority.
vocabulary: Rajput: member of one of several South Asian warrior and ruling communities
patron: a person who supports a writer, artist, or institution
source: Original summary based on The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Art of the Mughals before 1600

references.citation: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Art of the Mughals before 1600
